newsitem.title: USA: North Carolina cuts food tax, okays transit tax.
newsitem.headline: North Carolina cuts food tax, okays transit tax.

text.p: Negotiators in the North Carolina General Assembly have reached agreement on several tax proposals but remained at odds Friday over the budget.

Under an agreement reached Thursday, the state sales tax on food will be cut to 2 percent from 3 percent on July 1, 1998. The cut would reduce revenues by $90 million a year. Lawmakers opted to delay it until next year to allow the state to continue building up surplus revenues as a hedge against lean years.
The General Assembly cut the tax to 3 percent from 4 percent last year.
The sales tax cut was part of a package that also reduces inheritance taxes by 20 percent, reducing state revenues by $30.6 million a year.
The General Assembly also approved a bill allowing local governments to assess a $5 annual tax on motor vehicle registrations to improve mass transit.
It authorizes a Mecklenburg County referendum on a half-cent sales tax to expand its bus service and buy land for a commuter rail system.
It also allows the Triangle Transit Authority, which covers the Raliegh Triangle region in Wake, Durham and Orange counties, to impose a five percent car rental tax to fund a commuter rail system.

Despite agreement on the tax proposals, the Democrat-controlled Senate and Republican-controlled House were still trying to reach agreement on the $11.4 billion budget for the fiscal year that began July 1. They remain at odds over how to allocate state and federal welfare money.
They extended appropriations at fiscal 1997 levels for another week to allow the government to keep operating. The previous two-week extension was set to expire at midnight Friday.
The lawmakers also set a record Friday for the longest-running legislative session. North Carolina's previous record was set when the General Assembly adjourned on Aug 14, 1987.
